questions.stem: Market concentration refers to:
options: the number of consumers who buy a particular product in a single location
the share of a country's GDP produced by a single industry
the degree to which firms in a market sell identical products
the extent to which a market's sales are held by a small number of firms
questions.explanation: A concentrated market is dominated by a few large firms; an unconcentrated one has sales spread across many. Product similarity is a separate feature of market structure.

questions.stem: Market power is best defined as:
options: the legal right of a firm to be the only seller of a product in a market
the total value of a firm's sales in a financial year
the ability of consumers to choose between many sellers
the ability of a firm to influence the price or terms of trade
questions.explanation: A firm with market power can raise price above the competitive level without losing all its customers. It need not be a legal monopoly; a few large firms in an oligopoly also have it.

questions.stem: In a market, the four largest firms have shares of 30%, 25%, 20% and 10%. The four-firm concentration ratio is:
options: 30%, the share of the single largest firm
15%, the share held by all the smaller firms
85%, indicating a highly concentrated market
21%, the average share of the four largest firms
questions.explanation: The four-firm concentration ratio adds the shares of the four largest firms: 30 + 25 + 20 + 10 = 85%. A high ratio suggests an oligopoly with considerable market power.

questions.stem: A market has four firms with shares of 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), the sum of squared market shares, is:
questions.explanation: HHI = 40² + 30² + 20² + 10² = 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000. A single monopolist would score 100² = 10,000, while simply adding the shares gives 100.

questions.stem: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A one firm holds 65%; in Market B each of the four holds 20%. Which statement is correct?
options: The two markets are equally concentrated, as their concentration ratios are the same
Market B is more concentrated, as more firms have large shares
Neither market is concentrated, as no firm holds all the sales
Market A is more concentrated, which the HHI would show but the ratio does not
questions.explanation: The concentration ratio ignores how shares are spread among the top firms. Squaring shares in the HHI gives a far higher score to Market A, where one firm dominates.

questions.stem: Which market structure best describes an industry dominated by a few large firms with high barriers to entry?
options: Monopoly
Oligopoly
Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
questions.explanation: An oligopoly has a few large, interdependent firms protected by barriers to entry, as in Australian banking and grocery retailing. A monopoly has a single seller.

questions.stem: In a market, the fewer the firms and the larger their shares, the:
options: greater the market concentration and the likely market power
lower the market concentration and the likely market power
closer the market is to perfect competition
more elastic the demand each firm faces
questions.explanation: Concentration rises as sales are held by fewer, larger firms, which tends to give them more power over price. Many small firms with tiny shares are the mark of a competitive market.

questions.stem: Compared with a competitive market, a highly concentrated market is most likely to reduce allocative efficiency because firms:
options: have no control over the prices they charge customers
are unable to earn any profit in the long run
can restrict output and charge prices above the cost of production
must produce more than consumers want to buy in order to survive
questions.explanation: Firms with market power can earn higher profits by supplying less at a higher price, so too few resources flow to goods consumers value. Price takers are found in competitive markets, not concentrated ones.

questions.stem: Supporters of large firms in concentrated markets argue they can improve productive efficiency because:
options: large firms do not need to invest in new technology or equipment
economies of scale can lower average costs below those of many small firms
a lack of competition forces large firms to keep their costs as low as possible
concentrated markets always charge lower prices than competitive ones
questions.explanation: Large-scale production, purchasing and distribution can cut unit costs. Whether consumers gain depends on competitive pressure to pass on those savings, as weak competition can also allow costs to drift up.

questions.stem: Which argument links market concentration to higher dynamic efficiency?
options: Small firms cannot benefit from any innovation made by large firms
Large profits can fund research and development of new products and processes
Firms facing no rivals at all have the strongest incentive to cut their prices quickly
Concentrated markets prevent firms from changing their products over time
questions.explanation: Some economists argue that firms with market power have the funds and security to invest in innovation. Others argue that competitive pressure is the stronger spur, so the effect is debated.

questions.stem: When a new low-cost competitor enters a concentrated market, the most likely response of existing firms is to:
options: stop investing, as the new entrant will take all their customers
merge with the new entrant, as the law requires this
cut prices, improve service and seek ways to lower their costs
raise prices, as customers become more loyal to established firms
questions.explanation: Competitive pressure forces incumbents to respond on price, quality and cost or lose market share. This pressure is what drives productive and dynamic efficiency.

questions.stem: The entry of Aldi into Australian grocery retailing is often used as an example of:
options: how government ownership can reduce prices in a concentrated market
how a merger between two retailers can reduce market concentration
how a new entrant can increase competitive pressure in a concentrated market
how a market can move from monopoly to perfect competition in a few years
questions.explanation: A new entrant with lower costs pushed established supermarkets to respond on prices and private-label ranges. The market remained an oligopoly, but with more competitive pressure.

questions.stem: Which change is most likely to make a market more concentrated over time?
options: Online platforms that let small firms reach customers nationally
A series of mergers and takeovers among the existing firms
Lower start-up costs as new technology becomes cheap
The removal of licences that once limited the number of sellers
questions.explanation: Mergers combine firms, so fewer firms hold larger shares. Lower entry costs, deregulation and online selling all make entry easier and tend to reduce concentration.

questions.stem: Digital-only banks and new payment providers have entered Australian banking. In terms of market structure, this most likely:
options: turns banking into a perfectly competitive market almost overnight
creates a monopoly for the largest digital bank
has no effect, as only the number of branches matters
adds competitive pressure, though the market remains an oligopoly
questions.explanation: New entrants can challenge incumbents on fees and service, but high capital requirements, regulation and customer inertia mean a few large banks still dominate. Structure changes gradually rather than overnight.

questions.stem: Customers often stay with their bank even when rivals offer better rates. This inertia matters for competition because it:
options: means that banks face perfectly elastic demand for loans
reduces the pressure on incumbent banks to offer better prices
forces banks to cut their fees and interest margins quickly
makes it easy for new banks to win customers from incumbents
questions.explanation: If switching seems costly or troublesome, incumbent banks can keep customers without matching rivals. Policies that make switching easier aim to strengthen competition.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Australian banking industry best shows that it is concentrated?
options: Banks cannot differentiate their products, so they compete only on price
Four major banks hold most of the market for deposits and home loans
Many hundreds of small banks each hold a tiny share of the market
The government sets the interest rates that every bank must charge
questions.explanation: The four major banks dominate household banking, which is the hallmark of an oligopoly. Banks set their own lending rates, influenced by the cash rate and funding costs.

questions.stem: Australian grocery retailing is commonly described as an oligopoly because:
options: supermarkets must sell identical products at identical prices under the law
two large supermarket chains, with a few others, account for most sales
a single government-owned retailer supplies most groceries
many thousands of small grocers each hold a tiny market share
questions.explanation: A small number of chains, led by Woolworths and Coles, account for most grocery sales. Their size gives them power over both shoppers and suppliers.

questions.stem: A farmers' group and a supermarket chain both publish reports on supermarket profits. When using these sources, a student should:
options: consider each source's perspective and assumptions before drawing conclusions
accept the farmers' report, as suppliers are always the most reliable source
accept the supermarket's report, as businesses know their own costs best
ignore both reports, as only government data can ever be used
questions.explanation: Each group has an interest in how profits are presented, so their data and framing may differ. Comparing sources and checking assumptions gives a more balanced judgement.

questions.stem: Large supermarket chains have strong buying power over food suppliers. A social cost that may arise from this is:
options: lower profits for supermarkets, which reduces their tax payments
pressure on supplier prices that weakens investment by farmers and small producers
higher prices paid to farmers, which leads to the over-production of most foods
too many supermarkets opening, which wastes land and resources
questions.explanation: Dominant buyers can push down the prices they pay suppliers, which may squeeze suppliers' margins and investment. Shoppers may gain from lower prices, so judgements depend on perspective.

questions.stem: Petrol prices in some Australian cities rise sharply and then fall gradually in a regular pattern. This pattern is known as:
options: a petrol price cycle
a price ceiling
a cartel agreement
a price floor
questions.explanation: Price cycles are a feature of some retail petrol markets with a few large sellers. They are not themselves illegal; an agreement between rivals to fix prices would be cartel conduct.

questions.stem: Which is a private benefit of market concentration to the firms involved?
options: Higher prices paid to suppliers who sell to the large firms
Higher profits from the ability to set prices above competitive levels
Lower prices for consumers from intense price competition
More choice for consumers as many new firms enter the market and compete
questions.explanation: Market power lets dominant firms earn above-normal profits, benefiting owners and shareholders. Lower prices and more choice are features of more competitive markets.

questions.stem: A concentrated industry restricts output to keep prices high. Which outcome represents a social cost?
options: Higher employment in the industry than is socially optimal
Under-provision of the good, with a deadweight loss to society
Over-provision of the good, with too many resources in the industry
Lower prices for consumers, with losses for shareholders
questions.explanation: Restricting output means units that consumers value above their cost are not produced, a loss of allocative efficiency. Over-provision would be the opposite problem.

questions.stem: The main role of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is to:
options: enforce the Competition and Consumer Act and promote fair competition
set the cash rate to keep inflation within its target band
set the prices that all businesses must charge consumers
collect company tax from the large firms operating in concentrated industries
questions.explanation: The ACCC is the independent national regulator that enforces competition and consumer law. The RBA sets the cash rate, and the ATO collects tax.

questions.stem: Under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, cartel conduct includes:
options: a firm lowering its prices to win customers from rivals
a firm advertising heavily to build its brand
a firm offering loyalty rewards to its regular and new customers
rival firms agreeing to fix prices, share markets or rig bids
questions.explanation: Agreements between competitors to fix prices, restrict output, share markets or rig bids are prohibited, and serious cartel conduct is a criminal offence. Competing on price, advertising or loyalty schemes is lawful.

questions.stem: A firm with a substantial degree of market power engages in conduct that has the effect of substantially lessening competition. Under the Competition and Consumer Act, this is:
options: misuse of market power
lawful, as large firms may act as they wish
exclusive dealing approved by the ACCC
resale price maintenance
questions.explanation: Section 46 prohibits a firm with substantial market power from conduct with the purpose, effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition. Having market power is not illegal; misusing it is.

questions.stem: The ACCC finds that a company has engaged in cartel conduct. Which statement about penalties is correct?
options: The ACCC takes court action, and the court decides whether to impose penalties
The ACCC itself imposes any fine it chooses, without ever needing to go to court
The company's competitors decide the size of the penalty
Penalties can be imposed only by the Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: The ACCC investigates and brings proceedings, but penalties for serious breaches are imposed by the courts, such as the Federal Court. Criminal cartel cases are prosecuted by the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions.

questions.stem: Two large competitors in an already concentrated market propose to merge. Under Australia's merger laws, the ACCC is most likely to be concerned if the merger would:
options: lower the merged firm's costs through economies of scale
increase the number of products offered to consumers
lead the merged firm to invest more in new technology
substantially lessen competition in the market
questions.explanation: Acquisitions that would substantially lessen competition are prohibited, and mergers above set thresholds must be notified to the ACCC before they proceed. Cost savings may be weighed as a benefit, not a reason for concern.

questions.stem: The ACCC also monitors retail petrol prices and publishes reports on them. This mainly aims to:
options: improve information for consumers and keep pressure on sellers
set the maximum price each petrol station may charge
fix a single national price for petrol at every service station
collect fuel excise on behalf of the federal government
questions.explanation: Price monitoring exposes pricing patterns and helps motorists buy at cheaper times and places. It does not set prices; Australia has no national cap on petrol prices.

questions.stem: Queensland requires fuel retailers to report price changes within 30 minutes, and the prices are published through apps and websites. In economic terms, this:
options: reduces asymmetric information, so motorists can find cheaper fuel more easily
sets a price ceiling on fuel, so retail prices cannot rise above a set level
imposes a Pigouvian tax on fuel retailers who change their prices
gives one retailer a monopoly on publishing fuel prices
questions.explanation: Real-time price information lowers search costs, so buyers can switch to cheaper stations, increasing competitive pressure. It does not control the prices retailers choose to charge.

questions.stem: The mandatory Food and Grocery Code of Conduct, enforced by the ACCC, mainly aims to:
options: regulate how large grocery businesses deal with their suppliers
set the retail prices supermarkets charge for basic foods
ban supermarkets from selling their own private-label grocery brands
limit the number of supermarkets in each local area
questions.explanation: The code sets rules for dealings between large grocery businesses and suppliers, with penalties for serious breaches. It addresses the bargaining power of dominant buyers rather than setting shelf prices.

questions.stem: Rules that let bank customers securely share their banking data with rival providers are intended to increase competition mainly by:
options: requiring all banks to charge the same interest rate on home loans and deposits
preventing the major banks from offering new products to customers
transferring ownership of customers' accounts to the government
making it easier to compare offers and switch to new providers
questions.explanation: Data sharing reduces the information and switching costs that keep customers with incumbents, so rivals can compete for them. It does not set prices or restrict what banks may offer.

questions.stem: A government considers breaking up a dominant firm into several smaller competitors. A key argument against this strategy is that:
options: more firms always lead to higher prices for consumers
greater competition would reduce the incentive for every firm to innovate
smaller firms cannot be regulated under competition law
the smaller firms may lose economies of scale, raising average costs
questions.explanation: Splitting a firm may increase competition but can sacrifice cost savings from large-scale production. Evaluating the strategy means weighing these effects and the perspectives of consumers, owners and workers.

questions.stem: Which government strategy is most likely to increase competition in an oligopolistic industry?
options: Placing tariffs on imports that compete with local producers
Lowering barriers to entry, such as removing unnecessary licensing rules
Granting the largest existing firm an exclusive licence to supply the market
Approving mergers between the largest competitors in the industry
questions.explanation: Easier entry allows new firms to challenge incumbents, adding competitive pressure on prices and service. Exclusive licences, mergers among leaders and tariffs all reduce competition.
